newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Chretien in close race to retain seat.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien in close race to retain seat.

text.p: As he campaigns for his Liberal government's re-election on June 2, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien faces a tough fight with a Quebec separatist for his own parliamentary seat.
An opinion poll this week showed Chretien neck and neck with Bloc Quebecois opponent Yves Duhaime in the electoral district of Saint-Maurice, which includes his hometown of Shawinigan.

Duhaime represented the area from 1976 to 1985 for the Parti Quebecois, the separatist party that rules the French-speaking province. Duhaime and Chretien are fierce competitors known to dislike each other.
"It will be the clash of the titans. The Bloc Quebecois wants to win the riding at all costs, but Chretien won't let them walk all over him," local radio talk-show host Yvon Picotte told Reuters.

If the Liberals won the federal election and Chretien lost his seat, he would remain prime minister but would need to get elected in another district to sit in the House of Commons. Mackenzie King in 1945 was the last Canadian Prime Minister to win a national election but lose his own seat.
At Duhaime's nomination meeting on Thursday night, Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard, former leader of the Bloc Quebecois and Quebec's most popular politician, extolled the crowd to support Duhaime.
The Bloc Quebecois, which was the official opposition in the last parliament, aims solely to promote Quebec independence. It won 54 of the 75 Quebec seats in the 1993 federal election.
Bouchard said another strong separatist showing in Ottawa was needed to prepare for the next referendum on Quebec separation.
In October 1995, separatists lost a referendum on Quebec sovereignty by a razor-thin 50.6 percent to 49.4 percent vote.

Chretien, a 63-year-old lawyer who has been in politics for 34 years, most of them as the member for Saint-Maurice, has a reputation as the scrappy "little guy" from Shawinigan. Polls ahead of the 1993 election showed him in trouble in Saint-Maurice, but he ended up winning by 6,400 votes.

In this campaign, which Chretien called last Sunday, Chretien has been criticised for not doing enough to help the district, which has a 16 percent unemployment rate and 10,400 people living on welfare.
Saint-Maurice, 109 miles (175 km) northeast of Montreal, was once a bustling agricultural and industrial centre, with factories making paper and aluminum.
But in recent years, with many people leaving the area, residents have had to rely more on tourism.
Michel Dumaine, an undecided and unemployed voter, said Chretien simply has not been accessible.
"He has not been very visible over the last 3-1/2 years. That is my main criticism, but I will listen to what the two candidates have to say," Dumaine said.
Several voters said they had little interest in the election, and such a trend toward voter apathy could affect the outcome.
"At the factory, we are talking a lot more about the hockey playoffs than politics," said Claude Bournival, a printing plant worker.
